Metadata.title: Pisa
Metadata.description: A reality check for viral videos: is what you see physically possible?

Home.lede: Send a video of something falling, thrown or bouncing. Pisa measures its motion and tells you whether real gravity could have produced it.
Home.eyebrow: A physics check for viral videos

steps.title: How Pisa checks a video
steps.watching: Pisa finds the moment something falls, is thrown or bounces, and checks the camera is steady enough to measure.
steps.tracking: Meta's SAM 3.1 outlines the object in every frame, so its path is measured, not guessed.
steps.measuring: The path is tested against the laws of free fall. Air can slow a fall; nothing real slows down in mid-air.
steps.explaining: You get one of three answers, the numbers behind it, and the ghost to see it for yourself.

answers.physically_impossible: A law of motion is broken: the object slows down in mid-air, or speeds up faster than gravity allows.
answers.consistent_with_real_physics: Every law we check holds. That doesn't prove the video is real, only that its motion could be.
answers.inconclusive: Nothing in the clip can be measured reliably, so Pisa says so instead of guessing.

why.title: Why measure instead of asking a chatbot
why.gravityLabel: The gravity objects fall with in videos from today's generators. On Earth it is 9.81.
why.opinionLabel: Clean, real throws and bounces that a vision model tuned for physics accepted as plausible. Measuring the motion scored them 0.96 to 0.99.

scope.title: What Pisa checks
scope.checks: Falls, throws, bounces, and two objects dropped together.
scope.skips: Face swaps, lip-sync or cloned voices.

footer.built: Built for the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon with Muse Spark and SAM 3.1.

Check.title: Check a video
Check.scope: Pisa checks falls, throws and bounces. It does not check face swaps, lip-sync or cloned voices.
Check.fileHint: MP4 or MOV, up to 60 seconds and 50 MB.
Check.privacy: Pisa analyzes videos with Meta's AI models. While Pisa runs on hackathon credits, Meta may use what it receives to improve its models. Pisa deletes your video as soon as the analysis ends and keeps only the measurements.

explanations.slows_down_while_falling: The object slows down while it is still falling. Gravity and air can't do that.
explanations.acceleration_grows: The object speeds up faster and faster as it falls. Gravity pulls steadily, so real falls don't do that.
explanations.accelerates_upward: The object speeds up toward the sky, as if gravity pulled upward.
explanations.impossible: The way this object moves breaks a law of physics that every real fall follows.
explanations.consistent: The object speeds up at a steady rate as it falls, the way real gravity makes things fall.
explanations.weak_violation: Something in the motion looks off, but not clearly enough to call it impossible.
explanations.no_measurable_acceleration: The object moves at a steady speed, so there is no fall to measure.
explanations.depth_change: The object moves toward or away from the camera, which bends its path on screen too much to measure.
explanations.too_few_samples: The object is visible in too few frames to measure its motion.
explanations.no_measurable_events: Pisa couldn't find a fall, throw or bounce it could measure in this video.
explanations.pair_falls_apart: Two objects released together fall at different rates. Under real gravity they fall side by side, as Galileo showed.
explanations.bounce_gains_energy: The object leaves the bounce faster than it arrived. A real bounce always loses some energy.
explanations.gravity_changes: Gravity changes strength from one flight to the next. In a real video, even in slow motion, it stays the same.
explanations.camera_motion: The camera moves too much to measure the object against the background.
explanations.gravity_too_weak: The object falls as if gravity were weaker than on Earth. A slow-motion video looks exactly like this, so Pisa does not call it impossible.
explanations.gravity_too_strong: The object falls as if gravity were stronger than on Earth. A sped-up video looks like this, so Pisa does not call it impossible.
explanations.no_free_flight: Nothing in this video falls, flies or bounces on its own, so there is no motion Pisa can check.
explanations.too_unclear: Something falls, flies or bounces, but it is too small, blurred, hidden or brief to follow.

Result.consistentNote: This doesn't prove the video is real. It means the motion we measured breaks no law we check.

cards.accelerationDetail: Real falls speed up at a steady rate.
cards.fitDetail: Average distance between the measured path and the closest steady-gravity path.
cards.phasesDetail: Stretches of free flight between release, bounces and landing.
cards.bounceDetail: A real bounce keeps less than 100% of the speed it arrived with.
cards.pairDetail: One object's acceleration over the other's. Released together, real objects give 1×.
cards.gravityDetail: Strongest over weakest gravity across flights of one object. Real videos give 1×, even in slow motion.

cards.impliedGDetail: Real gravity on Earth is {earth} m/s². Slow motion makes it look weaker.

Privacy.title: Privacy policy
Privacy.lede: Pisa checks whether the motion in a video is physically possible. It needs your video only for as long as it takes to measure it.

what.title: What Pisa receives
what.body: The video you upload or forward, the language of the page or of your message and, on WhatsApp, your phone number so Pisa can reply. Pisa asks for nothing else: no account, no name, no location.

kept.title: How long it is kept
kept.body: Your video is deleted as soon as the analysis ends. The evidence video, which shows your frames with the measurements drawn on them, is kept for 24 hours so you can watch and share it, then deleted. Pisa keeps the result: the verdict, the measurements and the measured paths. They contain no image, sound or personal detail, and anyone with the result's link can open it.

models.title: Meta's AI models
models.body: To find what moves in a video and to word the result, Pisa may send it to Meta's AI models (Muse Spark and SAM 3.1). While Pisa runs on the credits of Meta's hackathon, Meta may use what it receives to improve its products. Copies uploaded to Meta are deleted from its storage when each call ends.

whatsapp.title: WhatsApp
whatsapp.body: Messages reach Pisa through Meta's WhatsApp Business Platform. Pisa uses your number only to reply: it is not saved with your result, and records keep only an unreadable form of it. So it never answers twice, Pisa keeps message identifiers, not their content, for 7 days.

browser.title: In your browser
browser.body: The website keeps your language in a cookie and your light or dark theme in your browser's storage. There are no analytics, advertising or tracking cookies.

services.title: Who runs it
services.body: The website runs on Vercel and the analysis on Modal; results and evidence videos are stored by Supabase. Each processes data only to run Pisa.

rights.title: Questions and deletion
rights.body: To ask a question or have a result deleted, open an issue on Pisa's public repository with the result's link. Results hold no personal data, but they are deleted on request.
